extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars interested in drama, literary theory and theatre history
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of the defining features, types, theoretical criteria, historical conventions, and theatrical devices associated with the dramatic genre of tragedy across cultures and periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre definition: tragedy as drama based on human suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is a genre of drama based on human suffering, specifically by way of terrible or sorrowful events that befall a main character or cast of characters. Traditionally the intention of tragedy is to invoke an accompanying catharsis for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the high-level defining criterion: subject matter should centrally involve suffering or grievous events; aim to produce a paradoxical response (pain that awakens pleasure) or catharsis. Examples cited include Greek, Elizabethan, naturalistic and modern tragic works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelian definition: enactment of a complete, important action
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: 'Tragedy is an enactment of a deed that is important and complete, and of [a certain] magnitude, by means of language enriched [with ornaments]... it is enacted, not [merely] recited, and through pity and fear it effects relief (catharsis)'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot must represent a whole (introduction, middle, ending) and be of sufficient magnitude; language and performance are central; the work should produce pity and fear leading to catharsis. Use this as a structural and affective standard when evaluating classical-style tragedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness and magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is characterised by seriousness and involves a great person who experiences a reversal of fortune (Peripeteia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tone and stakes should be grave; subject should involve events of significance (personal and/or public). In classical models the protagonist is often of high status to amplify moral and emotional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic reversal (peripeteia) and recognition (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal of fortune (peripeteia) is central; the tragic hero may also achieve a recognition (anagnorisis) — a change from ignorance to awareness about human fate, destiny, or bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective tragedies often structure the plot so that an action leads inevitably but unexpectedly to catastrophic results and to a revelation that reshapes meaning for hero and audience (e.g., Oedipus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia: error or frailty of the tragic hero
rubrics_metrics.description: The reversal of fortune must be caused by the tragic hero's hamartia, often translated as a character flaw or a mistake (an error rather than general depravity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic downfall should be attributable to a specific error or frailty—moral lapse, misjudgement, or mistake—rather than simple villainy or wholly external forces; Aristotle contrasts error-based tragedy with mere misadventure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis: emotional purgation for the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy effects through pity and fear the purification (catharsis) of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, consider whether the work elicits and resolves intense pity and fear, producing a sense of emotional release or ethical reflection in the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot complexity: complex vs simple plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's four species include 'complex' tragedy, which involves both peripety and discovery (peripety and anagnorisis), contrasted with simpler forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots combine reversal and recognition to produce stronger emotional and intellectual effects; assess whether the structure interweaves these devices or remains straightforward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal elements/unities (definition by formal elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: One subclass of definitions is 'definition by formal elements' (for instance the supposed 'three unities').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/neoclassical evaluative standards include unity of time, place, and action: a single plotline, compressed time frame, and unified locale. Use cautiously: many traditions (e.g., Shakespearean tragedy) deliberately defy these unities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition by situation, ethical direction, emotional effect (Mandel's subclasses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Oscar Mandel recognizes multiple ways to define tragedy: by formal elements; by situation (e.g., fall of a good man); by ethical direction (intellectual/moral effect); and by emotional effect (pity and fear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a work as tragic, consider which definitional lens is being applied—formal, situational, ethical, or emotional—and be explicit about the critical standard used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic subtypes: tragedy of circumstance, miscalculation, and revenge play
rubrics_metrics.description: Common forms include: Tragedy of circumstance (protagonists born into situations they don't choose), Tragedy of miscalculation (protagonist's error of judgement causes catastrophe), and Revenge play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify tragedies by causal logic: whether fate/circumstance, a personal error, or acts of revenge drive the plot. This influences expectations about agency, culpability, and moral framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character status and scope: classical nobility vs domestic tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical/Neoclassical tragedy typically features noble characters and affairs of state; domestic tragedy features ordinary middle-class or working-class protagonists whose downfalls concern private/domestic matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different historical models set different requirements for protagonist status. Modern approaches (e.g., Arthur Miller) accept ordinary people as tragic subjects; evaluate according to the chosen tradition's norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senecan style features (Renaissance/academic influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Senecan tragedies feature long declamatory, narrative accounts of action, obtrusive moralizing, bombastic rhetoric, detailed accounts of horrible deeds, long reflective soliloquies, ghosts, witches, revenge, suicide, blood and gore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or assessing works in Senecan-influenced modes, expect rhetorical emphasis, vivid descriptions of violence, moralizing commentary, and soliloquy-driven reflection rather than enacted spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical devices: chorus, masks, sung choral parts, ekkyklêma, mechane
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek tragedy used a chorus (sung/danced), masks, ekkyklêma (a wheeled platform to reveal off-stage action), and mechane (crane) to hoist gods—devices shaping how violence and the divine are represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how performance devices mediate what is shown vs reported; choices about onstage depiction, choral function, and machinery affect audience perception and can be purposeful constraints or expressive tools (e.g., use ekkyklêma for aftermath revelations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deus ex machina and its implications
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechane gave origin to the phrase 'deus ex machina'—the surprise intervention of an unforeseen external factor that changes the outcome of an event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a dramaturgical device, deus ex machina can resolve plots abruptly; many critical traditions view it as an anti-pattern undermining tragic inevitability, though it can be used deliberately for thematic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Racine/Corneille neoclassical precepts: nobility, affairs of state, moral restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Corneille held that the stage should feature noble characters and that tragedy deals with affairs of state; Racine condensed plots into tight sets of passionate, duty-bound conflicts between a small group of noble characters and concentrated on pathos and amorous passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neoclassical evaluation emphasizes unity, nobility of character, moral decorum (avoid depicting evil rewarded), and concentrated emotional conflict. Use these when assessing French classical-style tragedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shakespearean/Elizabethan features: psychological interiority and formal hybridity
rubrics_metrics.description: British tragedies of the Elizabethan/Jacobean periods diverged from classical models: they often defied the unities, blended high and low characters, adopted tragicomic tones, and emphasized interiority via soliloquy (exploration of fate, madness, agency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess such tragedies for psychological depth, hybrid structure, and moral/political complexity rather than strict adherence to classical unity and aristocratic-only protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modernist and post-classical criteria: expanded subject matter and skepticism about a single tragic model
rubrics_metrics.description: In modernist literature the definition of tragedy has become less precise; Aristotle's diktat that true tragedy depicts the high-born is often rejected—tragedy may depict ordinary people and address new social themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary evaluation should allow for pluralistic models: tragic effect may arise from social conditions, existential crises, or forms that blend comic/realistic elements; be explicit about theoretical stance when judging 'what counts' as tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hegelian tragic collision: conflict of ethical forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Hegel's theory frames tragedy as a conflict of ethical forces represented by characters (the 'tragic collision'), differing from Aristotelian hamartia-focused models and highlighting dialectical ethical conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Hegelian criteria to evaluate tragedies where antagonistic ethical systems collide and characters embody competing justified values—judge how the drama stages and resolves (or fails to resolve) that collision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nietzschean criteria: Apollonian and Dionysian balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Nietzsche saw tragedy emerging from the interplay of Apollonian (form, individuation) and Dionysian (ecstasy, dissolution) forces—a dual mood combining pain and pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work balances structured form and ecstatic, communal or elemental intensity; Nietzschean reading foregrounds metaphysical/aesthetic origins rather than plot mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance/contextual conventions (festival, contest, tetralogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Athenian tragedies were performed at state religious festivals as contests: playwrights presented tetralogies (three tragedies and a satyr play) in the open-air theatre, with all- male actors and a performing chorus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical production context shapes expectations (length, chorus function, public ritual role). Adaptations for modern stages may alter these conventions—assess fidelity or productive transformation of context.
